# Mahiḷāmukhajātaka (Ja 26)

**ID:** Ja 26
**Section:** Jātaka (ja)
**Collection:** Suttas-Late-1

**tipitaka.org (CST):** https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0513m.mul0.xml

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Mahiḷāmukhajātaka* (Ja 26) is a narrative in the Pali *Jātaka* collection opening with the verse incipit *Purāṇacorānaṁ vaco nisammā* [Fausböll 1877]. According to its frame story (*paccuppannavatthu*), the Buddha related the tale while residing at the Bamboo Grove (Veḷuvana) in Rājagaha concerning Devadatta, who had acquired patronage, gain, and a monastery at Gayāsīsa from Prince Ajātasattu, and a monk who had fallen under the influence of Devadatta's faction [Fausböll 1877; Wu 2012].

In the story of the past (*atītavatthu*), King Brahmadatta of Benares possesses an auspicious state elephant named Mahiḷāmukha ("Damsel-face") [Fausböll 1877, 1897]. After overhearing the violent conversation of thieves and murderers who gather near his stable, the normally gentle elephant becomes unruly, rampaging and killing his keepers [Burlingame 1921; Sarada]. The Bodhisatta, serving as the king's wise minister, deduces the cause of the elephant's sudden viciousness and arranges for virtuous sages and brahmans of self-control to converse about moral conduct nearby, which leads the elephant to regain his natural goodness [Burlingame 1921; Fausböll 1877; Sarada]. In the *samodhāna*, the elephant is identified as the misguided monk who associated with Devadatta's schism, King Brahmadatta as Ānanda, and the wise minister as the Buddha [Burlingame 1921; Fausböll 1877].
